description: FIREWATCH AI is a technology-driven team focused on developing AI-powered solutions for wildfire monitoring and early warning. We combine software engineering, AI, NASA satellite data, and interactive mapping to help detect, analyze, and understand fire events. We are looking for passionate teammates interested in AI, data science, GIS, frontend development, and environmental technology.
summary:
Wildfire responders receive two separate NASA hotspot feeds — VIIRS and MODIS — with no
quick way to tell which detections are the same fire seen twice and which are real. FireLink
reconciles both feeds into a single interactive map. Every hotspot is classified as
Confirmed (both satellites agree), Likely (one satellite plus a nearby detection from the
other), Single or Weak, and drawn with size, a white ring and a halo so the classes stay
readable without relying on colour. Users draw a box or type coordinates and immediately
get detection counts, an activity calendar that flags anomalous days and multi-day critical
periods, a multi-year monthly history compared with the long-term average, a burned-area
estimate in km² exportable as CSV or PDF, filters by satellite, fire radiative power and
brightness, NASA GIBS true-colour imagery, wind-driven spread direction, nearby protected
areas, shareable URLs that store coordinates and date, and automatic email alerts when a
region crosses a threshold. It also separates forest fires from agricultural burning. The
whole app runs from one Python file with no framework and no database.
details:
What it does
FireLink turns NASA FIRMS fire detections into a decision tool for people who have to act
on them. The user draws a box on the map or types west/east/south/north coordinates, picks
a date, and the app queries NASA FIRMS for both VIIRS (S-NPP) and MODIS. Instead of showing
two overlapping layers, it runs a reconciliation pass: detections from the two instruments
that fall inside the same pixel footprint and time window are merged into one fire event
with a confidence class — Confirmed, Likely, Single or Weak. The map colours detections by
fire radiative power using a colour-blind-safe palette and adds size, a white ring and a
halo, so severity is readable without colour alone.

Around the map, three tabs summarise the region: a burned-day calendar that marks days with
unusual activity and groups consecutive critical days, a history view with the monthly fire
count compared with the multi-year average and the anomaly, and a headline panel with the
number of fires, confirmed detections, peak intensity and a burned-area estimate in km².
Reports export to CSV and PDF. Optional layers add NASA GIBS true-colour imagery, wind
direction from OpenWeather so an alert can say which way a fire is spreading, and protected
or agricultural land so an alert states whether a fire is inside a reserve or on farmland.
Shareable URLs encode the box and date, and a built-in email notifier sends an alert when a
region crosses the configured threshold.

Why it matters
Two feeds, two answers, and no shared confidence is exactly the confusion that delays a
response. Merging them cuts duplicate reports, surfaces single-satellite fires that a
layer overlay hides, and gives an explicit confidence level for every alert. The burned-area
estimate and the CSV/PDF export plug straight into a situation report, and the calendar and
history views answer the question a land manager actually asks: is this normal for this
month or not? The app also distinguishes forest fires from agricultural burning, because
the response is different: a field being prepared is not an evacuation.

Tools, languages and technology
Python 3 standard library for the backend (http.server, no web framework), plain JavaScript
with Leaflet 1.9.4 and Leaflet.draw for the interface, canvas for the charts, and requests
for the NASA FIRMS HTTP API. No database and no build step: the app is one server file plus
one HTML page, so it runs anywhere Python runs, including a container.

Hardware and software used
A standard laptop for development, plus free hosting for the public demo. Only free and
open tools were used: Python, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap and CartoDB basemaps, NASA FIRMS and
NASA GIBS.

Creativity
The core idea is using satellite agreement as a confidence signal rather than drawing two
layers and leaving the interpretation to the user. That single decision drives the whole
interface: confidence classes, the alert levels, and the wording of the email alert. The
burned-area estimate is computed from the real pixel footprint of each instrument (VIIRS
0.1406 km², MODIS 1 km²) instead of a guess. The app also handles NASA's publication lag,
so a day that is still being published is labelled as partial instead of looking like a
quiet day.

Factors considered
Accuracy: every detection is traceable to its satellite, instrument, confidence and
brightness value. Accessibility: a colour-blind-safe palette, redundant shape and size
encoding, and readable contrast. Usability: the coordinate inputs and the GeoJSON upload
are visible, not buried in text. Performance: the interface stays responsive with thousands
of points by drawing on canvas. Cost: the entire stack is free and open source, so any
fire brigade can run it without a licence.
